ety.text: From Middle English yesterday, yisterday, ȝesterdai, ȝisterdai, from Old English ġiestrandæġ, ġister dæġ, ġestor dæġ, ġeostran dæġ (“yesterday”), by surface analysis, yester- + day. Cognate with Scots yisterday, yesterday (“yesterday”), Saterland Frisian jässendeeg, järsendeges (“yesterday”, adverb), West Frisian justerdei (“yesterday”), Dutch gisterdag (“yesterday”), dialectal German gestertag (“yesterday”), Swedish gårdag (“yesterday”), Gothic 𐌲𐌹𐍃𐍄𐍂𐌰𐌳𐌰𐌲𐌹𐍃 (gistradagis, “tomorrow”, adverb). Compare further Dutch gisteren (“yesterday”), German gestern (“yesterday”).

senses.d: The day immediately before today; one day ago.
ex: Today is the child of yesterday and the parent of tomorrow.
Yesterday was rainy, but by this morning it had begun to snow.

senses.d: The past, often in terms of being outdated.
ex: yesterday's technology
The worker of today is different from that of yesterday.
I started to watch the video yesterday, but could only finish it this evening.
I want this done yesterday!
I need it yesterday!

ety.text: Inherited from Old French ier, from Latin heri.

Proto-Indo-European *(dʰ)ǵʰyésder. Proto-Indo-European *(dʰ)ǵʰyési Proto-Italic *hezi Latin hereder. Latin herī Old Spanish yer Latin ab herī Spanish ayer Inherited from Old Spanish yer, eri, hier with the addition of the prefix a-, from Latin herī. Alternatively from Latin ab herī (“since yesterday”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese oonte (“yesterday”), from *ãoite, from earlier *anoite, from Latin ad noctem (“towards the night”), from nox (“night”). Displaced Old Galician-Portuguese eire. Cognate with Galician onte and Spanish anoche.

ety.text: From Middle English yes, from Old English ġīese (“by all means, of course, yes”), derived from the same root as yea. Compare Faroese júsá (“yes, indeed, certainly”).

senses.d: Used to show agreement or acceptance.
ex: Yes, you are correct.
Yes, you may go play outside now.

senses.d: Used to indicate disagreement or dissent in reply to a negative statement.
ex:
It was not my fault we lost the race.
Oh, yes, it was!

senses.d: Answer to a question presuming one answer when all answers are correct.
ex:
Do you like cake, or pie?
Yes.
(Countless examples can be found on the “Inclusive Or” subreddit, which is a forum dedicated to this joke.)

senses.d: An exclamation of pleasure or approval, usually transcribed with an exclamation point.
ex: Our second goal of the match! Yes!

senses.d: Response that confirms that the user is paying attention.
Used to ask for more information with a request.
ex:
I need some help.
Yes?

senses.d: An affirmative expression; an answer that shows agreement or acceptance.
ex: Was that a yes?
Yet a woman’s “yes” would have bound him to that other life forever, and made the thought of this savage existence repulsive.

senses.d: A vote of support or in favor of something.
ex: The workers voted on whether to strike, and there were thirty "yeses" and one "no".
Did he yes the veto?
"That's really what you wanted?" I yessed both; ...
“Heaven knows why a woman ‘Noes’!” / Clarrie nodded glumly. “And why she ‘Yesses’ in the end.”
"[…] Are you—?" / ". . . all right?" / We yessed simultaneously. / "At least, I think so."

senses.d: To attempt to flatter someone by habitually agreeing
There is; indicating the existence of something.
ex: Have you heard this before? "Nintendo 64 has no games!" Well, I did a little researching, and here's what I found: […]
[Message header:] No water... YES WATER! / We have water again!

senses.d: Indicating the possibility or allowance of something.

ety.text: First attested in 1380, from Old French oïl (1100), from Vulgar Latin *hoc ille or by surface analysis a compound of Old French o (affirmative particle) and il (“he”). Partially cognate to Occitan òc (“yes”) and Catalan oi (“isn't it?”). See the Old French term for details.
From Latin sīc. In the “yes” sense, from sīc (est).
